name: Artificial nose (17th-18th century plated metal)

image.caption: Plated metal artificial nose, 17th to 18th century. Front vi Wellcome L0058566

lead: Before modern rhinoplasty was common, people who had lost part or all of their nose could wear an artificial nose made of plated metal, giving the face a restored profile.
Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article pictures a 17th-18th century European example and says it would have been worn as an alternative to rhinoplasty.

paras: The prosthesis was worn on the face in place of surgical reconstruction.
Modern sources say autologous cartilage and bone grafts are preferred over artificial nose prostheses for augmentation because of lower rejection and complication rates.

angle.text: The device filled in a missing nose so the face looked whole while worn.

lead: A plated metal artificial nose from 17th-18th century Europe is pictured in reference works as a device that would have been worn as an alternative to rhinoplasty.[1] It restored the visual outline of the nose without surgery.

Surgical nasal reconstruction has a long history: the Sushruta Samhita describes a cheek flap, and Gasparo Tagliacozzi illustrated a reattachment technique in 1597.[1] Modern guidance prefers autologous grafts over prostheses for augmentation.[1]

paras: The plated metal nose served as an alternative to rhinoplasty.[1]
Tagliacozzi's Curtorum Chirurgia Per Insitionem (1597) illustrated a pedicle flap rhinoplasty; Carpue later published nasal reconstruction accounts.[1]
